question.text:
Find the inverse of the following matrix:

\[ A = \begin{bmatrix} 7 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 \end{bmatrix} \]
question.explanation:
Notice that the given matrix is diagonal.

The inverse of a diagonal matrix can be found as follows:

\[ \begin{bmatrix} a_{11} & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\ 0 & a_{22} & \cdots & 0 \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ 0 & 0 & \cdots & a_{nn} \end{bmatrix}^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{1}{a_{11}} & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{a_{22}} & \cdots & 0 \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ 0 & 0 & \cdots & \frac{1}{a_{nn}} \end{bmatrix} \]

In our case, we obtain

\[ A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 7 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 \end{bmatrix}^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{1}{7} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -\frac{1}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -\frac{1}{2} \end{bmatrix}. \]

\[ \begin{bmatrix} a_{11} & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\ 0 & a_{22} & \cdots & 0 \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ 0 & 0 & \cdots & a_{nn} \end{bmatrix}^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{1}{a_{11}} & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{a_{22}} & \cdots & 0 \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ 0 & 0 & \cdots & \frac{1}{a_{nn}} \end{bmatrix} \]

question.text:
Find the inverse of the following matrix:

\[ A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \]
question.explanation:
The given matrix can be obtained from the identity matrix by permuting its columns. Therefore, $A$ is a permutation matrix.

The inverse of a permutation matrix can be found as follows:

\[ P^{-1} = P^T \]

In our case, we obtain

\begin{align*} A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}^T = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1& 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0& 1 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

question.text:
Find the inverse of the following matrix:

\[ A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0& 1 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{3} & 1 \end{bmatrix} \]
question.explanation:
Notice that we're given a Frobenius matrix:

  • all entries on the main diagonal are ones

  • the matrix has only one column (the $2$nd column) where some entries below the main diagonal are not zeros

  • all the other entries outside the main diagonal are zeros

To find the inverse of a Frobenius matrix, we simply take the non-zero entries outside the main diagonal with opposite signs.

In our case, we obtain

\begin{align*} A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0& 1 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{3} & 1 \end{bmatrix}^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0& 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -\frac{1}{3} & 1 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

question.explanation:

  • all entries on the main diagonal are ones

  • the matrix has only one column (the $1$st column) where some entries below the main diagonal are not zeros

  • all the other entries outside the main diagonal are zeros

To find the inverse of a Frobenius matrix, we simply take the non-zero entries outside the main diagonal with opposite signs.

In our case, we obtain

\begin{align*} A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & 0& 1 & 0 \\ 7 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 0& 1 & 0 \\ -7 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}
